name: Postmodernism
summary: A building that quotes history in a joke and in colour: split pediments, giant keystones, pastel stone and a facade that works as a sign. Venturi, Graves and Johnson used it to answer the blank box of the Modern Movement.

philosophy.core_thesis: Architecture is communication: a building should carry meaning, memory and irony, and a decorated shed is better than a blank box.
design_principles: Quote a historical form in a changed scale, colour or material: a keystone 3 times too large, or a column in plywood.
Compose the front as a sign: a flat facade of 2 to 4 distinct layers, with the entrance and the title marked as a symbol.
Split and layer the classical elements: a broken pediment, a cut column, a loggia that is only a picture of a loggia.
Paint the building: use 3 to 5 flat pastel colours in large fields on stone, render and tile.
Combine two or more codes in one front, popular and learned, and let the contradiction show.
Make the entrance a stage: a tall arch or portal of 6 to 10m, with a bright lobby behind it.
anti_patterns: Blank, unadorned glass or concrete boxes
Faithful copies of a historical style with no irony
A single material and a single colour over the whole front
Structure shown as the main image of the facade
Rigid, purist geometry with no historical quotation
Facades with no sign, title or marked entrance

massing.form: A compact block or tower with a symbolic front, a gabled or arched top, and cut-away volumes and loggias.
massing.proportion: Blocks of 1:1 to 1:3; a tower has a tripartite division of base, shaft and top, in a ratio of about 1:3:1.
massing.roof: A broken pediment, a gable, a pyramid or a pitched top that serves as the logo of the building.
massing.relation_to_ground: A heavy base of stone or painted render, 1 to 2 storeys, and a stage-like entrance with steps and a portal.

structure.system: A concrete or steel frame hidden behind stone, stucco, tile or metal cladding.
structure.span_and_module: Standard office grids of 7.5 to 9m, hidden behind facades composed on a different, symbolic module.
structure.expression: The structure is not expressed. The facade is a cladding layer; its pattern is independent of the frame.

materials.finish: Smooth, bright and flat colour; surfaces are painted, tiled or polished, and read as a graphic layer.

facade.composition: A flat, layered front divided into base, middle and top, with oversize historical symbols and one clear entrance.
facade.openings: Square and arched windows in the middle layer, with a keystone or a surround; the window-to-wall ratio is 20 to 40%.
facade.solid_to_void: Solid leads: 60–80% opaque, painted in fields.

light_and_space.daylight: Daylight is even; in the atrium and lobby, skylights and coloured light turn the room into a stage.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A staged route: portal, then a high lobby or atrium, then rooms that quote a street or a piazza.
light_and_space.interior_character: Terrazzo floors, painted arches, laminate with graphic patterns, and a mix of historical furniture and bold new pieces.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is back as quotation and joke: it tells you what the building is and then laughs at it.

rules.rule: Use a classical symmetric front and break it with a witty twist.
Use pastel colour blocks on the facade for each element.
Exaggerate scale: an oversize keystone, column or window.
Mix classical references in one composition, and keep one idea clear.
Make the base, the middle and the top read as three clear tiers.

emotion.target_response: Wit and recognition: the viewer smiles at a familiar form that has been turned into a game.

avoid_when: The brief asks for restraint, honest structure or a timeless, quiet building.
The client wants a serious tone without any irony.

modifiers.how: Drop the pastel fields and the quotations, keep the layering of base, middle and top, and set the module to a regular 4 to 7m grid.

sources.title: Robert Venturi, Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (Museum of Modern Art, 1966)
Charles Jencks, The Language of Post-Modern Architecture (Academy Editions, 1977)
